en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
First Part
2.8 Section on Combinations (Samuccayavāra) How many offenses does a lustful bhikkhunī commit when she consents to physical contact with a lustful man?
A lustful bhikkhunī who consents to physical contact with a lustful man commits three offenses.
If she consents to being grasped below the collarbone and above the kneecaps, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika);
if she consents to being grasped above the collarbone and below the kneecaps, it is a grave offense (thullaccaya);
if she consents to being grasped at anything attached to the body, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When a lustful bhikkhunī consents to bodily contact from a lustful man, she incurs these three offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
By how many of the seven classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins do they originate?
Of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which legal issue is it?
Of the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*), by how many principles for settling are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures:
they may be a failure in virtue, or they may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within three classes of offenses.

It may be by way of the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), it may be by way of the class of grave offenses (thullaccaya), or it may be by way of the class of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is an issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what has been admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass … [and so on] … …pe….
How many offenses does one commit by asking for curd and then eating it?
One who asks for curd and then eats it commits two offenses:
she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when she accepts it with the thought, "I will eat it"; [she incurs a *pācittiya* offense when she eats it].
For every mouthful, there is an offense entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*):
by requesting curd and then eating it, she incurs these two offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
Of the seven classes of offenses, by how many classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins do they originate?
Among the four kinds of legal issues, to which legal issue do they belong?
By how many of the seven methods of settling are those offenses settled?
Those offenses belong to one of the four failures— namely,
failure in conduct (ācāravipatti).
Of the seven classes of offenses, they are comprised within two classes of offenses:
sometimes by the class of offenses entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*), and sometimes by the class of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from four origins.
It may arise from the body, not from speech or mind;
it may arise from both body and speech, not from the mind;
it may arise from both body and mind, not from speech.
They may arise from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is the legal issue arising from an offense.
Among the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles for settling.
It may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *paṭiññātakaraṇa*; it may be by means of both *sammukhāvinaya* and *tiṇavatthāraka*.
The eighth section on combinations is concluded.
